e: Inscriptions

The open data set of the Epigraphic Database Roma (EDR) contains 44,796 inscriptions found in Rome. For 30,124 of them the findspot is known (as a text description), and 37,209 are dated. By type: 37,275 epitaphs, 1,884 religious, 1,685 honorific and 1,027 building inscriptions; the rest are other or unknown (graffiti, seat inscriptions, fragments).
Inscriptions over time
The date is usually a period (“1st–2nd century AD”); the inscription’s weight is spread evenly over the 25-year bands of the period, as on the “Building activity over time” card.

Hover over a bar; click to set the map’s year slider to that time.

More than four-fifths of the inscriptions are epitaphs, and these are densest in the first half of the 1st century AD. This is when most of the great columbaria were built; in some, such as Livia’s and the Statilii’s, the slaves and freedmen of a single noble household were buried. The peak of honorific, religious and building inscriptions is later, the second half of the 2nd century AD and the early 3rd. The curves show the habit of setting up inscriptions, not the population; from the mid-3rd century the number of inscriptions falls sharply.

Epitaphs along the roads

Burial inside the city was not allowed in Rome, so tombs lined the roads leading out of it. From the names of roads, gates and catacombs in the findspot descriptions, 20,960 inscriptions can be assigned to a road; the bar shows the number of epitaphs.
